name: SYN Flood
description: A flood of TCP SYN packets, data size should be 0.
source_text:
11001 SYN Flood
A flood of TCP SYN packets, data size should be 0.

name: HTTP/S GET Flood
description: A flood of HTTP or HTTPS requests, designed to overwhelm web servers.
source_text:
51002 HTTP/S GET Flood
A flood of HTTP or HTTPS requests, designed to overwhelm
web servers.

name: UDP Flood
description: A flood of UDP packets, data size should be large or maximal, potentially targeting port 80 or 443.
source_text:
22003 UDP Flood
A flood of UDP packets, data size should be large or
maximal, potentially targeting port 80 or 443.

name: TCP RST Flood
description: A flood of RST packets.
source_text:
13004 TCP RST Flood
A flood of RST packets.

name: ICMP Flood
description: A flood of ICMP ping packets. Data size SHOULD be large.
source_text:
33005 ICMP Flood
A flood of ICMP ping packets. Data size SHOULD be large.

name: NTP Reflection Flood
description: An NTP Reflected flood the using MONLIST argument
source_text:
23006 NTP Reflection Flood
An NTP Reflected flood the using MONLIST argument

name: TCP PSH+ACK Flood
description: A flood of PSH+ACK packets. The data size SHOULD be small or zero.
source_text:
14007 TCP PSH+ACK Flood
A flood of PSH+ACK packets. The data size SHOULD be
small or zero.

name: TCP SYN+ACK Flood
description: A SYN+ACK flood targeting the handshake process to destabilize network connections.
source_text:
14008 TCP SYN+ACK Flood
A SYN+ACK flood targeting the handshake process to
destabilize network connections.

name: TCP ACK Flood
description: A flood of ACK packets. The data size SHOULD be small or zero.
source_text:
14009 TCP ACK Flood
A flood of ACK packets. The data size SHOULD be small
or zero.

name: TCP FIN Flood
description: A flood of TCP FIN packets. The data size SHOULD be small or zero.
source_text:
14010 TCP FIN Flood
A flood of TCP FIN packets. The data size SHOULD be
small or zero.

name: DNS Query Flood
description: A flood of DNS queries designed to overwhelm DNS servers with excessive requests.
source_text:
54011 DNS Query Flood
A flood of DNS queries designed to overwhelm DNS servers
with excessive requests.

name: UDP Multi-vector Flood
description: A combined attack using various UDP-based vectors to target different network vulnerabilities.
source_text:
24012 UDP Multi-vector Flood
A combined attack using various UDP-based vectors to
target different network vulnerabilities.

name: DNS Garbage Flood
description: A flood of UDP packets. DST Port must be 53. The data is garbage (not proper DNS request or reply). Data size SHOULD be large.
source_text:
24013 DNS Garbage Flood
A flood of UDP packets. DST Port must be 53. The data
is garbage (not proper DNS request or reply). Data size
SHOULD be large.

name: HTTP/S Flood Cookie Support
description: An HTTP Flood in which the attack tool is able to support cookie and respond to an HTTP 302 Redirect response.
source_text:
55014 HTTP/S Flood Cookie Support
An HTTP Flood in which the attack tool is able to support
cookie and respond to an HTTP 302 Redirect response.

name: HTTP/S Search Page Flood
description: An HTTP flood targeted at one or more search functions in the attacked website.
source_text:
55015 HTTP/S Search Page Flood
An HTTP flood targeted at one or more search functions
in the attacked website.

name: HTTP/S Login Flood
description: An HTTP flood aimed at login pages, designed to exploit resource-intensive processes.
source_text:
55016 HTTP/S Login Flood
An HTTP flood aimed at login pages, designed to exploit
resource-intensive processes.

name: HTTP/S Large File Download Flood
description: A targeted attack on large file downloads to consume significant bandwidth and server resources.
source_text:
85017 HTTP/S Large File Download Flood
A targeted attack on large file downloads to consume
significant bandwidth and server resources.

name: DNS Recursive Flood
description: A flood on DNS packet in which the subdomain is ever changing (1000.ddostarget.com, 1001.ddostarget.com)
source_text:
55018 DNS Recursive Flood
A flood on DNS packet in which the subdomain is ever
changing (1000.ddostarget.com, 1001.ddostarget.com)

name: HTTP/S Slow POST
description: Slow Post is an HTTP/S based low-and-slow DDoS attack using POST request with large Content-Length, however the attacker send the data byte-by-byte keep the connection ever open.
source_text:
85019 HTTP/S Slow POST
Slow Post is an HTTP/S based low-and-slow DDoS attack
using POST request with large Content-Length, however
the attacker send the data byte-by-byte keep the
connection ever open.

name: SSL Renegotiation
description: A low-and-slow HTTPS based attack. Using the SSL- Renegotiation option the attack causes the server to renegotiate the SSL that consumes large compute power.
source_text:
85020 SSL Renegotiation
A low-and-slow HTTPS based attack. Using the SSL-
Renegotiation option the attack causes the server to
renegotiate the SSL that consumes large compute power.

name: IPSEC Flood
description: A flood targeting IPSEC protocols and ports, aimed at disrupting secure communication channels.
source_text:
35021 IPSEC Flood
A flood targeting IPSEC protocols and ports, aimed at
disrupting secure communication channels.

name: HTTP/2.0 Continuation Flood
description: An attack using HTTP/2.0 continuation frames to exhaust server processing capacities by sending fragmented headers.
source_text:
85022 HTTP/2.0 Continuation Flood
An attack using HTTP/2.0 continuation frames to exhaust
server processing capacities by sending fragmented
headers.

name: Rapid Reset
description: A flood involving rapid resets of HTTP/2.0 connections, designed to destabilize communication and exhaust system resources.
source_text:
85023 Rapid Reset
A flood involving rapid resets of HTTP/2.0 connections,
designed to destabilize communication and exhaust system
resources.

name: Multi-protocol Flood
description: A complex flood that utilizes multiple protocols including ICMP, UDP, and TCP to achieve widespread network disruption.
source_text:
25024 Multi-protocol Flood
A complex flood that utilizes multiple protocols
including ICMP, UDP, and TCP to achieve widespread
network disruption.

name: HTTPS Flood Headless Browse
description: An HTTP/S flood in the attacking client is a headless browser and therefore encompasses all the technologies and libraries of a normal browser and can pass multiple standard DDoS mitigation challenges.
source_text:
55025 HTTPS Flood Headless Browse
An HTTP/S flood in the attacking client is a headless
browser and therefore encompasses all the technologies
and libraries of a normal browser and can pass multiple
standard DDoS mitigation challenges.

name: HTTPS Flood JavaScript Support
description: An HTTP/S flood in the attacking client is able to process JavaScript (JS) and therefore pass standard JS DDoS mitigation challenges.
source_text:
55026 HTTPS Flood JavaScript Support
An HTTP/S flood in the attacking client is able to
process JavaScript (JS) and therefore pass standard JS
DDoS mitigation challenges.

name: Multi-Vector Flood
description: A sophisticated attack that layers multiple types of flooding to target various aspects of network infrastructure simultaneously, aiming to exploit different vulnerabilities within the network stack. This flood operates across both application layer (Layer 7) and network/transport layers (Layers 3/4).
source_text:
56027 Multi-Vector Flood
A sophisticated attack that layers multiple types of
flooding to target various aspects of network
infrastructure simultaneously, aiming to exploit
different vulnerabilities within the network stack. This
flood operates across both application layer (Layer 7)
and network/transport layers (Layers 3/4).

name: UDP Amplification Flood
description: A UDP amplification attack that significantly increases the volume of incoming traffic to the victim by exploiting public-facing services.
source_text:
26028 UDP Amplification Flood
A UDP amplification attack that significantly increases
the volume of incoming traffic to the victim by
exploiting public-facing services.

name: QUIC HTTP/3 Flood
description: A flood utilizing the QUIC protocol and HTTP/3, designed to maximize efficiency and impact through high-speed, multiplexed connections.
source_text:
57029 QUIC HTTP/3 Flood
A flood utilizing the QUIC protocol and HTTP/3, designed
to maximize efficiency and impact through high-speed,
multiplexed connections.

name: Large Payload SYN Flood
description: A flood of TCP SYN packets with very large payloads, designed to overwhelm network equipment and processing capabilities. Also known as Tsunami Flood.
source_text:
17030 Large Payload SYN Flood
A flood of TCP SYN packets with very large payloads,
designed to overwhelm network equipment and processing
capabilities. Also known as Tsunami Flood.

name: GRE Flood
description: A flood using Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) protocols and ports, aimed at disrupting network communication channels.
source_text:
17031 GRE Flood
A flood using Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE)
protocols and ports, aimed at disrupting network
communication channels.

name: Pulse Wave / Hit & Run Flood
description: A series of brief, maximum-capacity volumetric bursts (lasting seconds to a minute) designed to suddenly shock network infrastructure, cause immediate resource exhaustion, and drop before automated mitigation defences can fully engage.
source_text:
454016 Pulse Wave / Hit & Run Flood
A series of brief, maximum-capacity volumetric bursts
(lasting seconds to a minute) designed to suddenly shock
network infrastructure, cause immediate resource
exhaustion, and drop before automated mitigation
defences can fully engage.

name: API Unformatted Payload Flood
description: A flood of raw, structurally invalid text, targeting public API endpoints, forcing the application gateway parser to consume excessive CPU cycles attempting to read or decode the unformatted incoming traffic.
source_text:
353007 API Unformatted Payload Flood
A flood of raw, structurally invalid text, targeting
public API endpoints, forcing the application gateway
parser to consume excessive CPU cycles attempting to
read or decode the unformatted incoming traffic.

name: API Formatted Unauthenticated Flood
description: A flood of syntactically correct and perfectly formatted JSON or XML payloads targeting public API endpoints that do not contain the authenticated session token (such as JWT).
source_text:
454015 API Formatted Unauthenticated Flood
A flood of syntactically correct and perfectly formatted
JSON or XML payloads targeting public API endpoints that
do not contain the authenticated session token (such as
JWT).

name: API Authenticated Request Flood
description: A flood targeting protected API endpoints utilizing valid authorization tokens (such as JWT or OAuth), successfully bypassing basic API gateway security filters and forcing backend applications to process resource-intensive database updates.
source_text:
55029 API Authenticated Request Flood
A flood targeting protected API endpoints utilizing
valid authorization tokens (such as JWT or OAuth),
successfully bypassing basic API gateway security
filters and forcing backend applications to process
resource-intensive database updates.

name: Non-HTTP/S Application Floods
description: Application flood that aren’t HTTP/S-based. For example, SIP Reflection Flood is a reflected amplification flood targeting Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) VoIP infrastructure.
source_text:
565032 Non-HTTP/S Application Floods
Application flood that aren’t HTTP/S-based. For example,
SIP Reflection Flood is a reflected amplification flood
targeting Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) VoIP
infrastructure.

name: Fragmented Network Floods
description: Network floods consisting fragmented packets with payload. Common examples are fragmented TCP packets containing the ACK flag, forcing the target’s stateful firewalls and deep packet inspection (DPI) systems to waste memory resources, or large UDP packets split across multiple IP fragments forcing network security devices to hold the fragments in memory buffers for reassembly, leading to buffer exhaustion.
source_text:
545033 Fragmented Network Floods
Network floods consisting fragmented packets with
payload. Common examples are fragmented TCP packets
containing the ACK flag, forcing the target’s stateful
firewalls and deep packet inspection (DPI) systems to
waste memory resources, or large UDP packets split
across multiple IP fragments forcing network security
devices to hold the fragments in memory buffers for
reassembly, leading to buffer exhaustion.
